directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; David Howard's dark bronze foliage holds its color best in full sun. Rich, warm apricot-orange decorative flowers contrast beautifully against deep bronze-purple foliage, a striking two-tone combination that has made this compact, long-blooming cultivar one of the most popular dark-leaved dahlias for both borders and containers since its introduction decades ago. Its shorter, bushier habit compared to many taller dahlia cultivars makes it well suited to the middle of a border or a large container, where its dark foliage provides season-long color even between flushes of bloom. Stake if grown in a windy site, deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, and in zones colder than 8, dig and store tubers indoors over winter after the first hard frost blackens the foliage.

directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Santa Claus dahlia produces large blooms and benefits from staking to support the heavy flower heads. Large, semi-cactus flowers are boldly striped and splashed with vivid red over a white base in an irregular, festive pattern that gives this cultivar its holiday-themed name, with no two flowers patterned quite identically, making each bloom a small surprise. Its bold, novelty bicolor pattern makes it a conversation-starting accent in a cutting garden or mixed border, standing out clearly against solid-colored dahlia companions. Stake individual stems to support the substantial flower heads, deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, and in zones colder than 8, dig and store tubers indoors over winter after the first hard frost.

planting.note: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Wine Eyed Jill is a collarette-type dahlia valued for its open, single-flowered, pollinator-friendly form.

directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Wine Eyed Jill is a collarette-type dahlia valued for its open, single-flowered, pollinator-friendly form. A single ring of bright yellow outer petals surrounds a distinctive inner collar of shorter, deep wine-red petaloids around a dark central disc, a two-tiered, open flower form characteristic of collarette dahlias that exposes the central disc to visiting pollinators far more than fully double dahlia forms. Its open, accessible flower structure makes it one of the better dahlia types for attracting bees and other pollinators, in addition to providing a distinctive, layered look for cut-flower arrangements. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, stake tall stems in windy sites, and in zones colder than 8, dig and store tubers indoors over winter after the first hard frost.

directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Nuit d'Ete's near-black flowers hold their deep color best with consistent moisture and moderate heat. French for 'summer night,' this decorative dahlia produces fully double, deep maroon-black flowers so dark they appear nearly black in most light, a dramatic, moody color that makes a striking contrast against paler companions in a border or cutting garden. Dark-flowered dahlias like this one are prized by cut-flower growers and designers for the sophisticated, deep contrast they bring to mixed arrangements, standing out distinctly among the more common bright pinks, oranges, and yellows of typical dahlia palettes. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, stake for support, and in zones colder than 8, dig and store tubers indoors over winter after the first hard frost.

directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Firepot is a waterlily-form dahlia with a compact habit well suited to smaller borders and containers. Flat, broad petals arranged in shallow, overlapping layers give this cultivar the distinctive waterlily flower form, colored in glowing shades of orange and gold that flicker like flame, a softer, less densely petaled bloom shape than fully double decorative or ball dahlias that shows off individual petals more clearly. Its compact size compared to many taller dahlia cultivars makes it a good choice for a smaller border or large container where towering dinner-plate dahlias would be out of scale. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering, and in zones colder than 8, dig and store tubers indoors over winter after the first hard frost blackens the foliage.

directions: Plant tubers or transplants after last frost in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; scarlet dahlia is a taller, more open-growing wild species than modern hybrid dahlias and benefits from staking. One of the wild dahlia species native to the mountains of Mexico and Central America that helped give rise to the thousands of modern hybrid dahlia cultivars grown today, it produces simple, single, brilliant orange-red to scarlet flowers with a yellow center on tall, airy, open-branched stems quite different from the dense, compact bushiness of most garden hybrids. Growing much taller than typical bedding dahlias and flowering later into fall, it offers gardeners a glimpse of the species' wild character and is valued by collectors and breeders for its genetic diversity and easy, prolific late-season bloom. Stake the tall, somewhat lax stems for support, deadhead to prolong bloom, and dig and store tubers over winter in zones colder than 8.
